hook.line: News stories and neighbourhood complaints are full of things that get dearer, darker or stronger. Spanish has one verb for each, built from the adjective, so you can say it in a single word.
hook.es: La subida del combustible encareció el transporte.
hook.en: The rise in fuel prices made transport more expensive.

examples.es: La subida del combustible encareció el transporte.
examples.en: The rise in fuel prices made transport more expensive.
The deal made the fares cheaper.

examples.es: La obra encareció el café del barrio.
examples.en: The building work made the neighbourhood's coffee more expensive.

rule:
English says "made it more expensive" or "made it darker": a helper verb plus an adjective. Spanish often squeezes that into one verb built from the adjective.

*caro* gives *encarecer*, *barato* gives *abaratar*, *oscuro* gives *oscurecer*, *fuerte* gives *fortalecer*.

The frame is simple: something happens, and as a result something else becomes that adjective. The thing that changes is the object: *encareció el transporte*.

The verbs follow normal patterns. The *-ecer* ones (*encarecer*, *oscurecer*, *fortalecer*) change like any other *-er* verb in the past: *encareció*, *oscurecieron*. The *-ar* one (*abaratar*) is regular: *abarató*.

When you meet a new verb that starts with *en-* or *a-*, look for the adjective inside it.
smallPrint: Teachers call these deadjectival verbs. The *a-* and *en-* prefixes (with *-ar* or *-ecer*) turn an adjective into "make it that way".

readAndPick.es: La subida del combustible encareció el transporte.

options: The deal made the fares cheaper.
The deals made the fares more expensive.
That deal made lunch more expensive.

readAndPick.es: La obra encareció el café del barrio.
options: The building work made the coffee more expensive.
The building work made the coffee cheaper.
The building work made the coffee darker.
The storm lit up the afternoon.

readAndPick.es: Caminar todos los días fortalece las piernas.
options: Walking every day tires your legs.
Walking every day makes your legs stronger.
Walking every day makes your legs thinner.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick the right verb and type the whole sentence: *La subida del combustible ___ el transporte.* (encareció or abarató)
yourTurn.answer: La subida del combustible encareció el transporte.
yourTurn.why: The fuel rise made transport dearer, so the verb comes from *caro*: *encareció*.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: The deal made the fares cheaper.
yourTurn.why: *Barato* gives *abaratar*, and one deal doing it gives *abarató*.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: The clouds darkened the sky.
yourTurn.why: *Oscuro* gives *oscurecer*; in the past it becomes *oscurecieron*.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: Exercise strengthens the muscles.
yourTurn.why: *Fuerte* gives *fortalecer*, and it is *fortalece* for one thing doing it.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: The building work made the neighbourhood's coffee more expensive.
yourTurn.answer: La obra encareció el café del barrio.
yourTurn.why: The thing that gets dearer, *el café*, is the object of *encareció*.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it about one deal: *La oferta abarató los pasajes.* Say: That deal made lunch cheaper.
Type in Spanish: The storm darkened the afternoon.

pitfalls.wrong: La subida hizo el transporte caro.
pitfalls.why: Understandable, but Spanish prefers the one-word verb built from the adjective.
Almost. *Abaratar* is an *-ar* verb, so the past ends in *-ó*, not *-ió*.
Almost. The verb is *oscurecer*, with the *-ec-* in the middle.
